sections.rule: One correct option. One mark each. No negative marking.
Enter the final figure only. No marks for working.
Match every pair. Two marks each. All or nothing.

paper.caselet: A cold-store owner runs at 95% occupancy for four months of the year and 30% for the other eight. A neighbouring plot is available. Adding a chamber would cost ₹1.4 crore, and the additional produce is available only in the same four-month window.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: The expansion is justified, because turning away produce in the peak is a lost sale
The new chamber would be idle for eight months, so its case rests on what the peak four months alone can cover
Occupancy averages about 52% across the year, so there is spare capacity and no case for building until the annual average approaches the physical limit of the site
The plot should be bought regardless, since land beside an existing site rarely becomes available twice and the option is worth more than the analysis that would delay it

paper.caselet: Moving a consignment by road costs ₹210,000 and takes 4 days. By rail and coastal shipping combined it costs ₹96,000 and takes 13 days. The consignment is a spare part held as insurance stock against a breakdown that halts a ₹40 lakh-a-day production line.
paper.stem: Which mode should be chosen, and on what basis?
options: Road, because the nine days saved are worth far more than the ₹114,000 difference given what a stoppage costs
Rail and coastal, because it is less than half the freight cost and the saving is certain while the breakdown it guards against may never happen at all
Rail and coastal, because slower modes are the correct default for heavy or bulky consignments
Either, since freight cost is the only figure that separates two modes carrying the same goods to the same destination in the same condition

paper.caselet: A firm's order-to-delivery time is 19 days. Measured stage by stage, actual work accounts for about 3 days; the rest is orders waiting for the next batch run, for credit approval, and for a weekly despatch window.
paper.stem: Where should the redesign start?
options: With the three days of actual work, because that is the part the firm directly controls
With the waiting between stages, since that is where sixteen of the nineteen days are
With the despatch window alone, since it is the last delay before the customer and therefore the one they actually experience
With adding capacity at each stage, so that work is completed faster everywhere

paper.caselet: A appliance maker promises next-day delivery on a range it has just widened from 40 to 260 variants, while keeping its existing quarterly production runs, single central warehouse and cheapest-quote carrier contracts.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: The promise and the operating design now describe different businesses, so one of the two has to move
The wider range is the problem on its own, and cutting variants back to 40 restores the position without touching the production runs or the warehouse
The carrier contract is the weak link, and re-tendering it will deliver the promise, since the days are lost in transit rather than before it
Nothing needs to change, because demand variability has not risen and the forecast is unchanged, and the uncertainty a chain absorbs is a property of its customers

paper.caselet: A firm sited four stockyards when road freight cost ₹4 per tonne-km and each yard could serve a 90 km radius economically. Freight is now ₹9 per tonne-km, the economic radius has fallen to about 55 km, and demand has grown in two districts that sit at the edge of two existing yards.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible response?
options: Keep the sites, because a stockyard is a long-lived asset and moving it destroys the investment already committed to building and equipping it
Re-run the siting decision on the new cost, radius and demand together, since all three inputs have changed
Add a yard in each of the two growing districts and leave the existing four unchanged
Close the two least-used yards, since higher freight cost makes fewer, larger sites cheaper to run and consolidation is the standard response to dearer transport

paper.caselet: A bakery makes a celebration cake for one weekend only. Each sells for ₹1,200 and costs ₹400 to make. Anything unsold is given away at the end of the weekend and returns nothing.
paper.stem: What does this cost structure imply about the quantity to bake?
options: Bake exactly expected demand, since that is the quantity which minimises the total mismatch cost on either side
Bake well above expected demand, because a missed sale costs twice what an unsold cake does
Bake below expected demand, because unsold stock returns nothing at all and a zero salvage value is the strongest argument for caution
The quantity cannot be decided without knowing how many were sold last year, since the costs alone cannot indicate a quantity

paper.caselet: A planner has used a smoothing constant of 0.1 for two years. A competitor's exit has permanently lifted weekly demand, and for six weeks the forecast has sat well below actual demand every week.
paper.stem: What should the planner do?
options: Switch to using last week's actual demand as next week's forecast until the gap closes, since the most recent figure is the best available estimate of the new level
Raise the constant so the forecast catches the level shift, accepting that it will also track noise more closely
Keep the constant, because a low value is what protects a forecast from over-reacting, and that protection is worth more than a faster response to any single run
Leave the method alone, since six weeks of error is normal variation around a forecast and reacting to a short run is how planners end up chasing noise

paper.caselet: A buyer is told the supplier has cut the fixed charge per order from ₹4,000 to ₹1,000. Annual demand and holding cost are unchanged.
paper.stem: What should happen to the order quantity, and why?
options: It should not change, because the order quantity is set by annual demand, which the supplier's charge does not affect in either direction
It should fall to a quarter, because the ordering cost has fallen to a quarter
It should fall to half, because the quantity moves with the square root of the ordering cost
It should rise, because cheaper ordering makes larger orders more attractive and the saving is best captured by buying in bulk

paper.caselet: A state has risen four places in the national logistics ranking. Its industry association reports that road quality and warehousing availability scores improved, while its members' own freight costs and delivery times are unchanged.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: The index measures the environment a supply chain operates in, so a better score need not yet show in firms' own costs
The ranking must be wrong, because the outcome that matters to firms has not moved, and a measure that does not track members' freight costs is measuring nothing useful
The improvement proves logistics performance has risen, and firms will be reporting savings shortly, since better roads and warehousing pass through to costs automatically
The index measures firm-level outcomes directly, so the two findings cannot both be true and one of the two reports has to be withdrawn

paper.caselet: A firm sources two components from one low-cost offshore supplier: a stable, high-volume fastener, and a fast-changing electronic module whose design revises every few months and whose demand swings sharply.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible sourcing change?
options: Move both onshore, because offshore sourcing carries disruption risk in every category, and that exposure settles the question ahead of any cost comparison
Keep both offshore, because the cost advantage applies to everything the firm buys, whatever the design revision rate or the demand pattern of the part
Move both to the responsive supplier, since a single relationship is simpler to manage and the coordination saved outweighs the premium paid on the stable part
Keep the fastener offshore and move the module to a responsive supplier nearer the market

paper.caselet: A retailer wants to cut delivery time to stores. It is considering three options: adding two regional warehouses, moving a third of volume from rail to road, or raising the safety stock held at the existing single warehouse.
paper.stem: Which reading of these three options is correct?
options: Whichever option costs least should be chosen, since each of them reaches the same delivery time and the decision is therefore purely a question of price
They are three different drivers of the same outcome, and the choice is a cost trade rather than a ranking
The warehouse option is the one that counts, because delivery time is decided by where stock sits rather than by speed
The transport change is always the best of the three, because moving faster is the only real lever on time

paper.caselet: Sales forecasts 40,000 units for the quarter, operations has capacity for 28,000 and plans to that, and finance has budgeted revenue on 36,000. Each number is circulated separately and none is reconciled before the quarter starts.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: Operations should build to 40,000, because the plan must serve whatever sales can sell
Sales should reduce its forecast to 28,000, since capacity is the hard limit and the rest is aspiration
The spread is acceptable because a forecast is uncertain and each function needs its own working figure
Three functions are committing the firm to three different quarters, and the reconciliation is the missing step

paper.caselet: A meal programme cooks 90,000 portions from one kitchen each morning and must deliver to 480 schools before 12:30. Cooking finishes at 07:30. Its 42 vehicles average 11 schools each per run, and last month 26 schools received meals after 12:30 on at least four days.
paper.stem: Where is the constraint on this operation?
options: In kitchen capacity, since 90,000 portions from one kitchen is the largest number in the case and scale of that order is what limits any operation
In the number of schools, since 480 destinations is more than 42 vehicles can reasonably serve
In the distribution window between 07:30 and 12:30, since cooking is already complete before dispatch begins
In the vehicles, since more of them would remove the late deliveries directly and additional capacity is the fastest route to serving the whole list on time

paper.caselet: End-customer sales of a household product have varied by about 5% month to month for two years. Retailer orders to the distributor vary by 20%, distributor orders to the manufacturer by 45%, and the manufacturer's production schedule by 70%.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: Each stage is adding distortion by ordering from the stage in front of it rather than from real demand
The manufacturer's planning is at fault, since its swing is the largest of the four and the biggest number in a chain marks where the problem is created
End demand must be more variable than the sales figures show, since orders reflect it and a 70% swing could not arise from demand varying by 5%
The pattern is expected, because orders further from the customer are naturally less accurate

paper.caselet: A fleet operator pays drivers a fixed sum per trip. Average round-trip time is 46 hours, of which 19 are spent waiting to load and unload. The operator is considering buying four more trucks to raise the number of trips completed each week.
paper.stem: What should be examined before the purchase?
options: Whether fuel cost per trip can be reduced, since that is the largest variable cost of a round trip
Whether the drivers can be paid more per trip, since faster driving would shorten the round trip
Whether four trucks is the right number, given that the fleet is the binding constraint
Whether removing part of the 19 waiting hours would raise trips per truck without buying anything

paper.caselet: A state wants to raise container throughput at a public port. Average vessel turnaround is 2.4 days against 0.9 at a nearby private terminal; the public port's cranes are older and its yard is congested, and the state has limited capital to invest.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible route?
options: Fund new cranes from the state budget, because ownership must stay entirely public for a strategic asset whatever the capital constraint the state is working under
Bring in private capital and operating discipline for the terminal while the state keeps the port's public role
Sell the port outright, since the private terminal already performs better on turnaround and ownership is what produced that difference
Accept the difference, because turnaround is decided by vessel size and cargo mix rather than by operations, so equipment and yard management cannot close it

paper.caselet: A component has stable annual demand, fixed cost per order, constant lead time, no discounts, and known annual holding cost.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Economic order quantity: Order a full year's demand in one lot, because a single ordering charge always beats twelve smaller ones whatever the holding cost turns out to be.
Economic order quantity: Use a newsvendor critical ratio to set the recurring order size, since both models choose a quantity under cost pressure.
Economic order quantity: Use EOQ for the lot size, and never let it answer the separate question of when replenishment must start.
Economic order quantity: Treat the EOQ quantity as the reorder point itself, so replenishment starts when stock falls to that number.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Exponential smoothing is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Exponential smoothing to the wider subject?
options: Once Exponential smoothing has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Exponential smoothing works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Forecast error is the signal; alpha controls how quickly planning responds without throwing away accumulated history.
Exponential smoothing improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.caselet: A retailer promises low prices and dependable availability but keeps many premium express facilities with duplicated stock.
paper.stem: Which diagnosis is best?
options: More facilities always improve both efficiency and responsiveness at the same time, so the network is already configured correctly for any promise.
Pricing and supply-chain choices are unrelated, because price is set in the market while cost is settled inside operations.
The only useful response is to add more product variety, since a wider range is what a low-price promise needs.
Its facilities and inventory choices may be more responsive—and costly—than the competitive promise requires, so the driver configuration lacks strategic fit.

paper.caselet: A firm sells one mature high-volume item and one volatile product with short life, high stockout cost, and frequent engineering changes.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Tailored sourcing portfolio: Choose suppliers on landed cost alone, without weighing disruption exposure or the obsolescence risk carried by a short-life product.

Tailored sourcing portfolio: Place both items with the longest-lead, lowest-price supplier, because a single consolidated relationship simplifies management and maximises volume leverage on unit price.
Tailored sourcing portfolio: Use a low-cost source for stable volume and a faster one for the volatile item, never one cost objective for every item.
Tailored sourcing portfolio: Reserve the responsive, collaborative source for the stable commodity and leave the volatile item on the slow low-price supplier.

paper.caselet: A retailer sells 8,000 units of a stable line each year. Placing an order costs ₹250 whatever its size, and holding one unit for a year costs ₹10.
paper.stem: What order quantity minimises the total of ordering and holding cost?
options: 800 units
400 units
283 units
632 units

paper.caselet: A components buyer supplies two lines. Line A is a mature part with high volume and stable weekly demand. Line B is a new variant with uncertain demand and frequent design changes. The buyer wants to consolidate both onto one offshore supplier to simplify management.
paper.stem: What does tailored sourcing say about that consolidation?
options: Consolidation is right, because a single supplier operating at scale lowers unit cost on both lines and simplifies coordination for the buying team.
Split them, because no single supplier suits every product: A fits a low-cost source and B needs a responsive one.
Move both onshore instead, since offshore sourcing is unsuitable wherever design changes are expected at all.
Keep both offshore but hold extra inventory of each, which covers the lead time without changing supplier.

paper.caselet: Retail sales move slightly, but retailer, wholesaler, and manufacturer orders show progressively larger peaks and troughs.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Bullwhip effect: Assume consumer demand moved by the same amount, and read the manufacturer's order swings as a true demand signal.
Bullwhip effect: Add more safety stock at every stage without addressing the order distortion that created the swings, since buffering is what inventory is there to do.
Bullwhip effect: Diagnose amplification across incentives, batching, forecast updates and lead times, since only a shared demand signal stops it.
Bullwhip effect: Ask each stage to optimise its own profit without sharing demand data, since local accountability serves the chain best.

paper.stem: How does India's use of shipping compare with the global pattern?
options: India ships a smaller share of its trade by volume than the world average, but a larger share by value.
India ships over 95% of its trade by volume against a global 80%, but only 65% by value against a global 70%.
India's volume and value shares are both close to the global figures, so its port profile is unremarkable.
India ships almost all of its trade by sea on both measures at once, which is what distinguishes it from other large coastal economies.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Six supply-chain drivers?
options: Six supply-chain drivers: Transportation speed alone determines supply-chain performance, because every other driver follows the delivery schedule.
Six supply-chain drivers: Each driver can be optimised independently, so the best network is the sum of six separate local optima.
Six supply-chain drivers: Adding facilities always lowers both total cost and total inventory, since local stock is cheaper to hold.
Six supply-chain drivers: Facilities, inventory, transportation, information, sourcing, and pricing jointly set the balance between responsiveness and efficiency.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Multimodal cost trade-off is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Multimodal cost trade-off to the wider subject?
options: A mode changes shipment size, time, handling, and stock as well as freight; total logistics cost joins those consequences.
Multimodal cost trade-off works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once Multimodal cost trade-off has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Multimodal cost trade-off improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.

paper.caselet: A plant needs monthly despatch to rise from 52,000 tons to 70,000. Three routes are on the table: redesign wagons to carry more per trip, add rakes to make more trips, or cut the 99-hour rake cycle so the existing rakes make more trips.
paper.stem: Why is the third route the one to take first?
options: Because railway agreements are easier to obtain than rolling stock, which makes it the fastest route to implement.
Because wagon redesign and extra rakes both raise fixed cost, and fixed cost is always the wrong lever in logistics whatever the throughput target.
Because it is the only route that increases throughput, the first two merely moving the same tonnage differently.
Because all of the extra throughput is already inside the existing cycle as waiting time, and the other two need capital and fresh stock.

paper.caselet: A student can state what LEADS index is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects LEADS index to the wider subject?
options: Once LEADS index has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen it, because a decision that keeps moving is not really a decision.
LEADS index improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system can be treated as somebody else's problem to solve later on.
A shared diagnostic makes system weaknesses visible and gives states a basis for coordinated improvement, not a guarantee of firm performance.
LEADS index works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Multimodal cost trade-off?
options: Multimodal cost trade-off: Handling and first or last-mile legs can be ignored, because both modes incur them equally.
Multimodal cost trade-off: Mode choice compares end-to-end transport, handling, port, inventory, lot-size, and service effects—not freight rate alone.
Multimodal cost trade-off: The lowest line-haul price is always the lowest total logistics cost, because freight dominates every other line.
Multimodal cost trade-off: Large sea lots never create inventory cost, since the goods are paid for only when they are sold.

paper.caselet: A rake cycle of 99 hours breaks down as loading 3.5 hours, idle before loading 7.5, waiting for a locomotive after loading 13, transit out 34, transit back 30, and unloading and readying about 9.75.
paper.stem: Which element is the largest single inefficiency to attack, as opposed to the largest block of time?
options: Transit out at 34 hours, which is the largest element in the cycle and therefore the biggest prize.
Waiting for a locomotive at 13 hours, which is detention created by the engine being reassigned elsewhere.
Idle time before loading at 7.5 hours, which is pure waiting and adds nothing to the movement.
Unloading and readying at about 9.75 hours, which is the element most directly under the plant's control.

paper.caselet: Two customer groups buy one product. One group accepts delivery any time within a few days. The other needs it inside a narrow window each morning.
paper.stem: Which customer-profile attribute separates these two groups?
options: Order size, since a customer needing a fixed time is usually buying in smaller quantities.
Timeliness, which is a separate attribute from response time and is what decides the design here.
Reverse logistics needs, since tighter delivery windows generate more returns and repeat visits.
Cost sensitivity, because a narrow delivery window is a premium service and is priced as one.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Sales and operations planning is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Sales and operations planning to the wider subject?
options: Sales and operations planning improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Once Sales and operations planning has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Sales and operations planning works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Forecasts become decisions only when demand is reconciled with the real cost and flexibility of capacity, inventory, and service.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Transport turnaround?
options: Transport turnaround: Throughput can rise only by buying more wagons, since the number of vehicles owned sets the ceiling on annual movement capacity.
Transport turnaround: Turnaround improves asset throughput by removing waiting from the full trip cycle; Rajashree targeted locomotive detention so the same rakes could make more trips.
Transport turnaround: Idle waiting after loading does not affect annual capacity, because the wagons are already loaded and the tonnage has already been committed to a customer.
Transport turnaround: Loading speed is the only time that matters in a rail cycle, because a rake starts earning again the moment it is full.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Tailored sourcing portfolio is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Tailored sourcing portfolio to the wider subject?
options: Once Tailored sourcing portfolio has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Tailored sourcing portfolio improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Different demand and product risks require different source capabilities; a portfolio prevents one cost objective from governing every item.
Tailored sourcing portfolio works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Akshaya Patra meal logistics is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Akshaya Patra meal logistics to the wider subject?
options: Public service quality is completed at the recipient, so production, routing, timing, and safety must hold together end to end.
Akshaya Patra meal logistics works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Once Akshaya Patra meal logistics has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Akshaya Patra meal logistics improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.caselet: Last period's forecast was 100, actual demand was 120, and alpha is 0.25.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Exponential smoothing: Move the next forecast upward by 25% of the 20-unit error, giving 105.
Exponential smoothing: Move the forecast down to 95, applying the 25% adjustment against the direction of the error.
Exponential smoothing: Keep it at 100, because smoothing averages past demand and never responds to a single period's error.
Exponential smoothing: Set the next forecast to 120, because the latest actual replaces the old forecast entirely.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Ports and PPP?
options: Ports and PPP: Private participation automatically removes every maritime constraint, so oversight of service performance can be withdrawn once the investment arrives and the equipment is installed.
Ports and PPP: Container traffic can move at scale without hinterland links, because a terminal's own handling capacity sets its throughput by itself.
Ports and PPP: Port performance is determined only by whether the terminal is publicly or privately owned, and nothing else moves the number.

Ports and PPP: Ports support trade and coastal movement; public-private participation can add capacity and operating capability, but performance still depends on connected infrastructure and governance.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains LEADS index?
options: LEADS index: It ranks countries rather than Indian states and union territories, so it cannot guide state-level policy.
LEADS index: A high score proves every firm in the state has low logistics cost, since the index measures realised firm outcomes.
LEADS index: It is a direct count of warehouse square footage and nothing more, so a state improves its score by building sheds.
LEADS index: LEADS uses stakeholder perceptions and operating indicators to compare state logistics strengths and improvement areas and encourage policy competition.

paper.caselet: A network adds stockyards and vehicles, yet orders remain late because loaded assets wait at every organisational hand-off.
paper.stem: What should be investigated first?
options: Only the purchase price of the new vehicles, since asset cost is what the investment case turns on.
End-to-end cycle time and hand-off coordination, because idle detention can consume capacity despite more physical assets.
A larger safety-stock target at every node, because more stock at each point protects the delivery promise.
Removal of shared performance measures, so each site is judged only on what it controls directly.

paper.caselet: A forecast rises sharply, but the plant has long training times and cheap storage.
paper.stem: What should planning do next?
options: Use the forecast directly as the production order without checking capacity, since the forecast is what the plant has committed to deliver.
Ignore inventory entirely, because forecasting and operations are separate functions that hand work to each other in sequence.
Fire and rehire workers each period regardless of training cost, because output should track demand exactly month by month.
Translate the forecast into a capacity-and-inventory plan, likely using stable capacity with inventory and limited flexibility rather than blindly chasing demand.

paper.caselet: Secondary delivery becomes more expensive than primary line-haul and dealers require an overnight service radius.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Stockyard location trade-off: Minimise primary line-haul distance while leaving secondary delivery cost out of the comparison entirely.
Stockyard location trade-off: Re-evaluate site locations using the changed cost structure, coverage limit, demand, and minimum throughput together.
Stockyard location trade-off: Keep the existing sites, because demand locations alone determine where a stockyard belongs, whatever has since changed in transport cost or coverage limit.
Stockyard location trade-off: Consolidate into one large site regardless of dealer distance, since fewer sites always mean lower total network cost.

paper.stem: What are standing charges in a chartered-shipping cost build-up?
options: The demurrage that becomes payable when loading or unloading runs beyond the laytime agreed in the charter.
The cost of hiring the vessel for the period, which accrues whether or not it is moving.
The port fees charged for a berth, which are levied once per call regardless of tonnage handled.
The fixed component of the barge operating cost, prorated across the days the barges are actually worked.

paper.caselet: One vehicle carries containers for fourteen to eighteen schools on a fixed route. The meal has to still be hot at the last stop.
paper.stem: How should the vehicle be loaded?
options: Heaviest containers first, so the load is stable and the vehicle can be driven at route speed.
In the order the containers left the kitchen, which keeps the staging area and the loaded vehicle in step all morning.
Last in, first out: the first school on the route is loaded last, never by what is convenient at the kitchen.
By school size, largest first, so the biggest deliveries are cleared while the food is at its hottest.

paper.caselet: A stem gives annual demand, a figure of ₹90 described as a cost, and a second figure of ₹4 also described as a cost.
paper.stem: How should the two cost figures be assigned to K and h?
options: The larger figure is always the ordering cost, since a fixed charge levied per order exceeds the cost of holding a single unit for a year.
Assign them either way and take whichever assignment produces the smaller order quantity, which is the safer policy.
Only the units separate them: currency per order is K, currency per unit per year is h, and the size of the figure decides nothing.
The figure quoted first is K, because a stem states the fixed cost before the variable one.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Ports and PPP is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Ports and PPP to the wider subject?
options: A port is a transfer node, so capacity creates trade value only when sea-side operations and inland flows work together.
Once Ports and PPP has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Ports and PPP works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Ports and PPP improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.caselet: Marketing promises high variety and same-day availability while operations uses slow transport, long batches, and suppliers chosen only for low price.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Strategic fit: Add more product variety and same-day options without changing transport, batch sizes, or supplier selection, because the promise made to the customer is a marketing decision.
Strategic fit: Measure suppliers only on unit purchase price and ignore availability, because the lowest landed cost defines a fit supply chain.
Strategic fit: Redesign the chain for the promised responsiveness or change the promise, because performance always fails when the two diverge.
Strategic fit: Keep both strategies unchanged, because each function is already locally efficient on its own budget and targets.

paper.caselet: A buyer places one pre-season order for a printed festive range. Demand for the print is uncertain, there is no chance to reorder once the season starts, and unsold stock is cleared at well below cost afterwards.
paper.stem: Which model does this description specify, and which clause settles it?
options: Aggregate planning, settled by the seasonal pattern, which is what a chase, flexibility or level strategy is chosen against each season.
Exponential smoothing, settled by the uncertainty in demand, which is what a forecast exists to handle.
The newsvendor model, settled by there being one buying opportunity with no replenishment and a salvage value below cost.
Economic order quantity, settled by the fact that stock is being ordered in a batch rather than continuously.

paper.caselet: An efficient operator considers a new city with different commodity flows, trader relationships, seasonal demand, and refrigerated transport needs.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Cold-storage expansion: Decide from the price of available land alone, treating construction cost as the whole of the expansion question.
Cold-storage expansion: Copy the current facility exactly, because management skill transfers automatically to any market the operator enters.
Cold-storage expansion: Test local utilisation, commodity fit, economics and financing first, because cold capacity pays only when all of them hold.
Cold-storage expansion: Assume the new capacity stays full throughout the year, so a single peak-season utilisation figure can carry the case.

paper.caselet: A loaded rake waits an average 13 hours for a locomotive, limiting monthly trips despite adequate loading capacity.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Transport turnaround: Coordinate an engine-on-load arrangement and accountability for the hand-off so detention falls and trips per rake rise.
Transport turnaround: Increase factory output while loaded wagons continue to stand idle, because production volume is what limits despatch.
Transport turnaround: Buy additional rakes before addressing the 13-hour wait, since more assets must produce more trips.
Transport turnaround: Measure only tonnes loaded per wagon and ignore cycle time, since a fuller wagon is always a more productive one.

paper.caselet: A seller must choose one order for a short season; leftovers are discounted and unmet demand loses contribution and goodwill.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Newsvendor decision: Use EOQ, because the item is inventory and a lot-size formula applies to any stocking decision.
Newsvendor decision: Order the mean forecast quantity regardless of margin and salvage value, since the average is the best single estimate.
Newsvendor decision: Use a critical-ratio decision based on underage and overage costs to select the demand quantile.
Newsvendor decision: Ignore lost margin because only leftover stock carries a visible cost at the end of the season.

paper.caselet: A regional warehouse forecast 1,200 units for last month. Actual demand came in at 1,320 units. The smoothing constant in use is 0.2.
paper.stem: A regional warehouse forecast 1,200 units for last month. Actual demand came in at 1,320 units. The smoothing constant in use is 0.2.
paper.prompt: What is the forecast for this month?

paper.stem: Match each prompt to the precise explanation or action.
choices: Move the next forecast upward by 25% of the 20-unit error, giving 105.
Exponential smoothing updates the old forecast by a fraction alpha of the latest forecast error; a larger alpha reacts more strongly to recent demand.
Use a level plan and draw inventory down, since a forecast becomes a decision only when reconciled with capacity cost.
S&OP balances forecast demand with capacity, utilisation, inventory, backlog, and outsourcing over a medium-term horizon.

paper.stem: Match each prompt to the precise explanation or action.
choices: Use a critical-ratio decision based on underage and overage costs to select the demand quantile.
The newsvendor model chooses a one-time quantity under uncertain demand by balancing the cost of one unit too few against one unit too many.
EOQ chooses an order size that balances annual ordering cost against holding cost under stable demand, lead time, price, and no-shortage assumptions.
Use EOQ for the lot size, and never let it answer the separate question of when replenishment must start.

paper.stem: Match each prompt to the precise explanation or action.
choices: A sourcing portfolio matches responsive sources to volatile, high-value or time-sensitive items and efficient sources to stable, predictable volume while managing disruption risk.
Use a low-cost source for stable volume and a faster one for the volatile item, never one cost objective for every item.
The bullwhip effect is the amplification of order variability upstream even when end-customer demand changes only modestly.
Diagnose amplification across incentives, batching, forecast updates and lead times, since only a shared demand signal stops it.
